source: Freedman, Dejl, Gorur, Yin, Rago, Toni (2024/2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification
finding: ArgLLMs ask the model for one supporter and one attacker per claim (depth 1) or recursively (depth 2), score each argument 0-1, and let code compute the claim score with DF-QuAD gradual semantics. The answer is true if score > 0.5. Accuracy is about equal to chain-of-thought, not better.
numbers: Datasets TruthfulClaim, StrategyClaim, MedClaim (200-sample pilot for prompt choice). Models: Mistral, Mixtral, Gemma 7B, Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3 8B, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o mini (+GPT-4o on MedClaim). Example cells in Table 1: Gemma 7B CoT 0.79 vs Est.Base Arg D=1 0.81; Mistral CoT 0.70 vs 0.68; Mixtral CoT 0.72 vs 0.70 vs 0.5-Base 0.56.
quote: even powerful models have relatively limited zero-shot capabilities in argument generation and estimation
limits: Binary true/false claims only. Claims were LLM-generated then hand-checked. Large variation across prompts per model and dataset. Authors say zero-shot argument generation is limited.
agent_relevance: S7-style selection by code over model-written pro/con arguments costs little accuracy and makes the decision path auditable. It does not raise accuracy by itself. Treat it as a faithfulness tool, not a correctness tool.

source: Freedman, Dejl, Gorur, Yin, Rago, Toni (2024/2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification
finding: Key design choice: letting the model give the root claim its own confidence (Est. Base Arg) beats giving the claim a neutral 0.5. With a neutral root the verdict comes only from model-written arguments and falls below baselines.
numbers: Across the 3 datasets and 7 models, 0.5-Base-Arg rows are typically 0.03 to 0.17 below CoT; Est.Base rows are within about 0.03 of CoT in most cells. Depth 2 (7 arguments) did not reliably beat depth 1 (3 nodes).
limits: Depth effect inconsistent. Only DF-QuAD in main text; quadratic energy semantics in supplement.
agent_relevance: If the schema computes survival by code, the prior (the model's own pre-argument estimate) must be an input. Otherwise the attack graph throws away information the model already has.

source: Freedman, Dejl, Gorur, Yin, Rago, Toni (2024/2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification
finding: Faithfulness and contestability: the final score is a deterministic function of the arguments and base scores, so a human can change one argument's strength or add an attacker and the output moves in a provable direction. Two formal contestability properties are defined and DF-QuAD satisfies them.
numbers: Formal result, no N. Example: adding an attacker to an attacker counts as pro for the parent and cannot lower its score.
limits: Proof is for tree-shaped QBAFs with DF-QuAD. Whether humans actually contest well was not user-tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Gives G2 (revise from real output) a mechanism: edit the single failing node and recompute, no re-sampling.

source: Zhou, Dejl, Freedman, Chen, Rago, Toni (2025) Evaluating Uncertainty Quantification Methods in Argumentative LLMs
finding: Swapped the confidence estimator inside ArgLLMs. Plain direct prompting (rate your confidence in this argument) beat more complex uncertainty methods (LUQ, Semantic Entropy, Eccentricity).
numbers: 500 samples per dataset; gemma-2-9b-it, Llama-3.1-8B, GPT-4o-mini (4-bit for open models); TruthfulClaim, StrategyClaim, MedClaim; D=1,2; 0.5 and estimated base score. Of 180 pairwise bootstrap CIs (5000 resamples), 74 were significant; 44 favoured direct prompting, 24 LUQ, 6 Semantic Entropy, 0 Eccentricity. Biggest gap: StrategyClaim Gemma-2, 0.5 base, D=1, 0.130 above next best. Direct prompting was never beaten by more than 0.028.
limits: Single run per cell. Semantic Entropy not available for GPT-4o-mini.
agent_relevance: Cheap self-rated strength per node is enough. Do not spend budget on sampling-based uncertainty for each argument node.

source: Ng, Jiang, Freedman, Rago, Toni (2025) MArgE: Meshing Argumentative Evidence from Multiple LLMs for Justifiable Claim Verification
finding: Merge argument trees from several small LLMs into one QBAF and compute the verdict by code. This beats single LLMs, single-model ArgLLMs and free-form multi-LLM debate with a GPT judge.
numbers: Datasets Truth/Strategy/Med Claim. Versus Debate (open LLM pairs + GPT-4o-mini judge): MArgE up to 8.4 points better, at most 2.6 worse in two cases; MArgE-D1 beats all Debate setups in 6 of 9 settings. With GPT-4o-mini as scorer, up to about 20 points over earlier baselines; beats GPT-4o-mini CoT by 3.5 and 1.0 points on two datasets, loses on MedClaim. Debate accuracy swings with model order (Truth: 0.676 to 0.808). MArgE max SD over 3 runs 0.019. Also scoring the root claim adds about 13.31 points (+-1.83).
limits: Gains partly rely on a stronger scorer model. Domain knowledge (Med) from small open models limits it. Three runs only.
agent_relevance: Supports code-side aggregation over structured arguments from several sources instead of a model judge (G5). The diversity here is across different models, which G4 says matters; samples from one model would not give this.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) ArgRE: Formal Argumentation for Conflict Resolution in Multi-Agent Requirements Negotiation
finding: ArgRE (requirements negotiation) turns each proposal, critique and refinement from LLM agents into an argument, the conflicts into attacks, and a solver computes the grounded and preferred extensions. Accept or reject is by code, with a traceable justification.
numbers: 5 case studies, 30 runs. Decision Justification Score 4.32 vs 3.07 (p<0.001, independent raters). BERTScore F1 94.9%, statistically indistinguishable from heuristic ablation. Compliance coverage 84.7% vs 47.6% and 47.8% for baselines. Trace Completeness 40.9% average. Default pairwise protocol gives acyclic graphs (Graph Cyclicity Index = 0) where grounded = preferred; cross-pair arbitration gives GCI about 0.25 and the two semantics diverge.
limits: Ratings by evaluators on a few cases; compliance coverage partly a function of generation volume. No test of whether accepted requirements are more correct.
agent_relevance: A working example of an LLM loop where attack edges come from the model and survival comes from a solver. Model-made graphs are mostly acyclic, so grounded is enough and cycles are rare.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) QUARE: Quality-Aware Requirements Analysis through Multi-Agent Dialectical Negotiation
finding: Same line of work with Dung-style argumentation in a multi-agent pipeline. Reports large coverage gains but a lower conflict resolution rate than the baseline, which the authors explain as finer conflict detection.
numbers: Compliance coverage 98.2% vs 47.6% (MARE) and 47.8% (iReDev); semantic preservation 94.9%; verifiability 4.96/5; conflict resolution rate 25.0% vs MARE 66.7% and iReDev 46.7%; 25-43% more requirements generated.
limits: Metrics partly favour verbose output. Lower resolution rate means more conflicts surfaced but fewer settled.
agent_relevance: More attack edges found does not mean better answers. Count what survives, but also check it against an outside test (G3).

source: Li, Fang, Chen, Li, Liao (2024/2025) Enhancing Conflict Resolution in Language Models via Abstract Argumentation
finding: Zero-shot chain-of-thought LLMs are poor at computing Dung extensions. After supervised fine-tuning on solver-generated step-by-step explanations they become near perfect, and the explanations matter for generalising to larger graphs.
numbers: Before training Qwen2.5 CFP 0.71 (complete) and 0.78 (preferred), ALSE 0.62 and 0.63; Llama3 CFP 0.51 and 0.45, ALSE 0.42 and 0.48. After SFT Qwen2.5 CFP 1.00 / ALSE 0.99 (complete), 1.00 / 0.95 (preferred); Llama3 1.00 / 0.99 and 1.00 / 0.86.
limits: Training, not a scaffold. Synthetic AFs. Preferred-semantics accuracy does not exceed GNN solvers. Failure modes named: hallucination, early termination.
agent_relevance: Do not ask a prompted model to compute the grounded extension in its head; compute it in code. If it must be done in text, step-by-step IN/OUT/UNDEC labelling is the format that works.

source: Li et al. (2025) Enhancing Conflict Resolution via Abstract Argumentation (generalisation and noise)
finding: Models trained without step explanations collapse on larger frameworks than seen in training; models trained with explanations degrade gradually. Noisy training steps (half of a step's IN set replaced at random) hurt Pass@k.
numbers: No-explanation models fell as low as 30% accuracy in the generalisation stage; explanation models stayed relatively high but declined as complexity rose.
limits: Noise test only for grounded semantics.
agent_relevance: A single wrong step propagates to the final extension, so a model-run solver needs per-step checking. Code removes the risk.

source: Steging, Renooij, Verheij (2025) Parameterized Argumentation-based Reasoning Tasks for Benchmarking Generative Language Models
finding: Dynamically generated attack graphs turned into witness-testimony puzzles (Alice says the train is late, Bob says Alice lies). Models must decide if a target statement holds. Models fail even on simple linear chains and are brittle on non-linear graphs.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-flash/pro, Claude-3.5-haiku/sonnet, o1-preview. Linear chains: answer is yes for odd length, no for even; most non-o1 models over-answer yes; GPT-4o-mini, Gemini flash and pro fall toward the 50% baseline as chains grow; o1-preview 100% on every linear length (first 75 prompts). 2,540 non-linear prompts, correct answer yes in only 8.85%; Claude-3.5-sonnet best overall, GPT-4o higher precision. o1-preview made mistakes on the hard non-linear subset though precision stayed 100%.
limits: Natural-language witness story, not formal notation. Per-model table rows only partly legible in text extraction. o1-preview tested on a subset.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that models do not reliably evaluate attack chains in text. Supports giving the attack graph to code and not to the model.

source: Steging et al. (2025) parameterized benchmark, order effect
finding: Argument order changes answers. Shuffling the arguments moved MCC up for some models and down for others. GPT-4o seems to presuppose the first argument it reads and reasons top to bottom.
numbers: Shuffled non-linear prompts: GPT-4o MCC +8.14, Claude-3.5-sonnet MCC -16.48; MCC rises for GPT-4o and Gemini-flash, falls for Claude haiku and sonnet, unchanged for GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-pro. In non-linear graphs with 15 arguments GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-sonnet do worst near two directed paths and best with few or many.
limits: Single benchmark family generated by the authors.
agent_relevance: A cheap code test for the schema: re-order the candidates and attacks and confirm the survivors do not change (a symmetry check as in G3).

source: Sanayei, Vesic, Blanco, Surdeanu (2025) Can LLMs Judge Debates? Evaluating Non-Linear Reasoning via Argumentation Theory Semantics
finding: Given only the flattened debate dialogue, LLMs rank arguments by acceptability. Agreement with QuAD gold ranks is low to moderate, drops with longer debates, and improves with chain-of-thought and examples.
numbers: NoDE datasets: DebatePedia (short debates) and 12AngryMen (3 acts; Acts 1-2 have 4x and 3x more arguments than Act 3). Models gpt-4o, claude-3, command-r-plus, llama-3; 3 runs, temperature 0.7. DebatePedia: vanilla Spearman about 0.11, CoT few-shot 0.46 (tau 0.42). 12AngryMen overall: vanilla rho 0.11 / tau 0.08; ICL one-shot 0.24 / 0.17; CoT zero-shot 0.31 / 0.24; CoT few-shot 0.35 / 0.26. Act 2 vanilla rho -0.02. About 24% lower rho and 38% lower tau on 12AngryMen than DebatePedia. GPT-4o DebatePedia CoT few-shot 0.54 / 0.50.
limits: Acyclic graphs only. QuAD only. The gold is a formal proxy for acceptability, not human judgment. Position and length biases reduced but not removed.
agent_relevance: Models cannot recover which arguments win from raw text; even the best prompt gives rho near 0.5 on short debates. This is why explicit edges plus code (S7) should beat asking the model to judge.

source: Sanayei et al. (2025) Can LLMs Judge Debates? (edge recovery and biases)
finding: Models were also asked to rebuild the signed edge set from dialogue. Advanced prompting reduces length and position bias in rankings. Edge match counts only if both endpoints and polarity are right.
numbers: Graph-level precision, recall and F1 macro-averaged per split; per-model values are in the paper's tables and were not copied here.
limits: Edge recovery numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: The weak step is edge extraction, not the final compute. Spend verification effort on the attack edges.

source: Gorur, Rago, Toni (2024) Can Large Language Models perform Relation-based Argument Mining?
finding: Few-shot primed chat LLMs classify a text pair as attack or support better than the RoBERTa baseline across ten datasets, but attacks are harder than supports for every model.
numbers: Macro F1: Llama 70B-4bit 75 (best), Mixtral 8x7B-4bit 73, Mistral 7B 70, Llama 13B 62, Llama 13B-4bit 64, RoBERTa baseline 68. Inference time per pair: 1.73 s (Llama 70B-4bit), 0.28 s (Mixtral), 0.06 s (Mistral 7B). Priming uses four fixed labelled examples. Best LLM top on seven of ten datasets.
limits: Binary task (no no-relation class). English only. No fine-tuning. Quantised models. Attack F1 lagged support F1 in nearly all rows.
agent_relevance: Edge labelling by an LLM is workable, but attack edges are the weak point. Add a second check on every attack edge that decides a survivor.

source: Alfano, Greco, La Cava, Monea, Trubitsyna (2026) LLM-based Argument Mining meets Argumentation and Description Logics
finding: Pipeline: Qwen2.5 7B extracts arguments, attack and support relations and initial fuzzy strengths from a raw debate; quadratic-energy gradual semantics propagate strengths in code; results go into a fuzzy description-logic knowledge base for querying.
numbers: Extraction mix in one corpus: 45.60% attack and 34.72% support relations (7.17% and 1.08% of them targeting arguments); another corpus 32.64% attack and 45.60% support. One annotator agreement step reached F1 0.92. Authors state results are independent of which gradual semantics is chosen.
limits: Demo scale; no accuracy against human-labelled acceptance outcomes. Qwen2.5 7B only.
agent_relevance: Shows the pattern LLM edges + code semantics + query, but gives no evidence that the final ranking is correct.

source: Bhargava, Tonelli, Martin-Rodilla (2026) Have You Been Convinced? Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning (NARS) for ChangeMyView
finding: LLM-extracted bipolar argument graphs from long ChangeMyView threads, propagated with gradual semantics, predict whether the original poster changed their view only weakly, though better than zero-shot reasoning LLMs.
numbers: CMV2BAS n=384. Best NARS ensemble F1 0.5682, AUC about 0.56 (bootstrap CIs about +-0.05 to 0.06, overlapping across configurations). Random: accuracy 0.5025, F1 0.5266. Logistic regression on 4 graph features: accuracy 0.5392, F1 0.5635, AUC 0.5869. Zero-shot Qwen3.6:27B F1 0.2525 (accuracy 0.4914, AUC 0.5227); GPT-oss:20B F1 0.1341 (accuracy 0.4674). Adding structure and strength scores to the LLM prompt lifted F1 only to 0.2660 and 0.1639.
limits: NARS is barely above random and not clearly above a plain logistic-regression baseline. Failure modes: support-dominant threads and long chains weaken attack propagation. Delta labels are noisy.
agent_relevance: An honest negative: formal propagation over model-made graphs gave weak predictive power on real, noisy argument. The attack graph is only as good as the extraction.

source: Fungwacharakorn, Zin, Nguyen, Kong, Satoh (2025) Argumentative Reasoning with Language Models on Non-factorized Case Bases (AAM-CBR)
finding: Abstract argumentation for case-based reasoning with LLM agents: models decide case coverage and extract factors; the symbolic AA-CBR step gives the outcome. It beats a single-prompt baseline only when the new case has many factors.
numbers: Synthetic credit-card data. Gemini-2.0-flash-lite: AAM-CBR 0.28 (default outcome 0) at n=6 factors vs single prompt 0.76; at n=10 AAM-CBR 1.00 / 0.96 vs best single prompt 0.90 for outcome 1. GPT-4o: n=10 AAM-CBR 0.98 / 0.96 vs best baseline 0.80 for outcome 1; baselines better at n=6. Case factor extraction accuracy about 0.80 given a relevant case. Relevance judgement is biased toward relevant; chance a case is truly relevant is 2^(n-10).
limits: Small synthetic dataset. The crossing point depends on n.
agent_relevance: Symbolic layer helps when many items interact; for small cases the model alone is as good or better. The model over-calls relevance, a bias toward linking too much.

source: Li, Russo (2026) Leveraging LLMs for Causal Discovery: a Constraint-based, Argumentation-driven Approach (ABAPC-LLM)
finding: LLMs are used as imperfect experts: their proposed required and forbidden edges enter an assumption-based argumentation framework alongside data tests, and the solver keeps the best jointly defensible subset, so wrong LLM constraints get defeated.
numbers: Metrics SHD, precision, recall, F1 vs ground-truth DAGs on synthetic semantically grounded random graphs and bnlearn graphs. Example in LT graphs: MPC-LLM gains 0.09 F1 and cuts SHD by 1.91 over MPC; ABAPC-LLM gains 0.035 F1 and cuts SHD by 0.60 over ABAPC. ABAPC-LLM is conservative: best SHD and recall on average, MPC-LLM sometimes higher F1. Slower because of solver time; extension reasoning is NP-complete in the grounded ABA setting.
limits: Competitive, not dominant. Memorisation bias handled with a new protocol using synthetic graphs.
agent_relevance: Concrete use of attack-based arbitration where model suggestions can be overridden by an independent signal (data). Matches G3: a model claim loses to evidence.

source: Mileva, Bikakis, D'Asaro, Law, Russo (2023/2025) A Unifying Framework for Learning Argumentation Semantics
finding: Inductive logic programming learns interpretable acceptability semantics for abstract and structured frameworks. Compared with deep-learning solvers (Craandijk and Bex 2020) it reaches perfect accuracy for some semantics while staying readable.
numbers: Reports Matthews correlation 1 for some semantics. No LLM is used. Exact solvers like ASPARTIX stay the reference.
limits: Only partly read (intro and results sections). No LLM comparison.
agent_relevance: The survivor computation is cheap and exact (ASP or a solver); there is no need for a model inside it.

source: ArgLLM-App (2026) An Interactive System for Argumentative Reasoning with LLMs
finding: A web system implementing ArgLLM agents for binary tasks, with visual explanations, user contesting of arguments, and external trusted sources.
numbers: Abstract only; no accuracy numbers.
limits: Abstract seen via arXiv page only.
agent_relevance: ArgLLM is moving to interactive use; contestation is the selling point, not accuracy.

source: Authors (2026) Can One-sided Arguments Lead to Response Change in Large Language Models?
finding: Giving a model one-sided arguments steers its stated opinion across diverse models, topics and argument counts. Switching to other arguments consistently decreases steering.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract.
agent_relevance: Models accept whatever arguments are in the prompt. An agent loop that shows only the attackers of one candidate will bias the verdict. Show both sides and hide authorship (G5).

source: Authors (2025) Echoes of Agreement: Argument Driven Opinion Shifts in Large Language Models
finding: Supporting or refuting arguments in the prompt shift model positions toward the argument in single- and multi-turn use; stronger arguments give higher directional agreement. The authors read this as sycophancy.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract.
agent_relevance: A model's verdict on whether A defeats B will follow the argument it is shown last or strongest. Use code, or blind the judge.

source: Authors (2026) Consistency Is Not Validity: Self-Rewarded Moral Argumentation Makes Language Models Decisive but Pliable
finding: RL on self-judged pairwise argument quality makes models more decisive and more invariant to option order, but sycophancy and reframing sensitivity remain.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract.
agent_relevance: Order consistency can be optimised without improving validity; supports outside checks.

source: Large Language Models in Argument Mining: A Survey (2025)
finding: Survey: prompting and CoT blur argument-mining subtask boundaries; notes the risk of evaluation circularity when LLMs both annotate and judge, and long-context robustness as an open problem.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract.
agent_relevance: Warns against grading model-built graphs with model judges.

source: Authors (2024) Assessing Open-Source Large Language Models on Argumentation Mining Subtasks
finding: Mistral 7B, Mixtral 8x7B, Llama2 7B and Llama3 8B tested on argumentative discourse unit classification and relation classification, zero- and few-shot, on Persuasive Essays and Microtexts.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers read.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract.
agent_relevance: Small open models vary widely on relation classification, which feeds the attack edges.

source: Dung (1995) On the acceptability of arguments and its fundamental role in nonmonotonic reasoning, logic programming and n-person games
finding: Founding paper. An argumentation framework is a set of arguments and one attack relation. Grounded, preferred and stable extensions are defined; the grounded extension is the least fixed point of the characteristic function and is computable in polynomial time. Links to stable models in logic programming.
numbers: From prior knowledge; no numbers.
limits: Not opened this session. Claims come from background knowledge, not a page read.
agent_relevance: Grounded semantics is cheap and unique, so S7 can compute survivors deterministically. Preferred and stable need search and may give several answers.

source: Background on complexity and learned solvers (Dunne and Wooldridge; Craandijk and Bex 2020), as cited by open papers
finding: Skeptical acceptance under preferred semantics is hard in the general case (NP- or Pi2-complete class), grounded is polynomial. Graph neural networks (AGNN) were trained to approximate semantics. 2412.16725 reports its fine-tuned LLM matches but does not exceed GNN accuracy for preferred semantics.
numbers: Complexity classes are standard knowledge, not read here as primary sources.
limits: Not opened as primary sources.
agent_relevance: For graphs of agent scale (tens of nodes) an exact solver is instant; no approximation needed.
